prize_parts.citation: for the invention of the optical lattice clock, in which atoms trapped at a magic wavelength are interrogated without a light shift, and for its realisation at the 10^-18 level

statement.case_for: My preferred configuration is unchanged: a single prize for Katori and Ye on the optical lattice clock. After the first round I am more, not less, convinced, because no member has argued that the two-name credit is wrong or that the clock lacks independent reproduction, while every competing candidate carries a problem that its own proponents admit. The physical picture is simple. Atoms held in a standing wave of light are normally shifted by that light, which ruins the spectroscopy. Katori saw that at a particular wavelength the shifts of the two clock levels cancel, so thousands of atoms can sit still, free of Doppler and recoil effects, and be probed together. Ye's group then showed what the idea could do at the state of the art, with 10^-18 systematic uncertainty and with the many-body coherence of the lattice. Laboratories in Japan, the USA, Germany, France and China have built such clocks and compared them, and the agreement is reproduced across groups. The clocks resolve the gravitational redshift over a millimetre and bound the variation of constants. In answer to the chair's first question, I propose the citation above. It names the magic-wavelength lattice and the light-shift cancellation, so that it is separated from the 2005 comb prize and the 2012 prize on single trapped quantum systems. It does not say that NIST, PTB, SYRTE and others did nothing. It credits the concept and its record-level realisation, which is a claim the record supports.
statement.case_against: I take the dissent of Ulf and Olle seriously and have not dismissed it. The lattice clock is a measurement advance, and a better instrument is not the same thing as a new phenomenon in nature. The null results on drifting constants mean that the fundamental-physics payoff is so far prospective, and the second has not yet been redefined. Lemonde, Takamoto, Derevianko, Ludlow and the NIST, PTB and SYRTE groups made real contributions to the theory of the shifts and to the accuracy evaluations, and a two-name prize cannot reflect them. I also work in this field and have a bias towards precision atomic physics, so I have asked myself whether I am rewarding familiarity. My answer is that the support comes from members with different specialities, which reassures me. The alternative that I find most interesting scientifically, B013 on the quantum boundary, is less mature and has diffuse credit, and B004 and B017 have problems of attribution and maturity that were not resolved in round 1.

responses.point: Ulf holds that B004 is a discovery with a clear before and after, while he sees the lattice clock as instrumentation whose fundamental-physics payoff is mostly promised. He also says that B004 would be settled once the question of discovery is answered.
responses.response: I accept the distinction between a new phase of matter and a better clock, and for me it is a real one. But I would not put the lattice clock wholly on the instrument side. Putting many atoms in a lattice at a magic wavelength opened a regime in which the atoms themselves are the object: many-body coherence, interaction shifts and spin-orbit effects in the lattice are physics in their own right, and the millimetre-scale redshift is a direct observation of gravity on a laboratory sample. On B004, the credit question is not only a matter of settling the discovery question. You concede that Bernevig, Hughes and Zhang proposed the HgTe realisation, and the three-person limit does not allow them. I cannot see how the citation would avoid inviting the objection that the committee chose the wrong theorists. You also say the 2016 prize touched the same lineage. If you can name a trio and a citation limited to the Z2 state and its observation that satisfies you, I would put B004 as my first alternative, which is where I have it. I do not think it beats B041 this year.

responses.point: Olle prefers B017 as a prediction followed by an experimental discovery, argues that the unresolved pairing mechanism should not delay recognition (comparing high-Tc), and says he may be giving too much weight to his own field when optical lattice clocks have unquestionable maturity.
responses.response: I appreciate your candour, Olle, about the maturity of the clocks. On the pairing mechanism, your comparison with the high-Tc cuprates is fair. The cuprates were recognised long before the mechanism was understood. The difference I see is that in 1987 the phenomenon was stable: a material with a certain transition temperature. In magic-angle graphene, what counts as the discovery is still shifting, because the phase diagram depends on the twist angle, on strain and on the substrate, and groups differ on the nature of the insulating states. Eight years is also short next to a lattice clock that has been compared across continents for nearly two decades. I would be more comfortable if a citation limited itself to flat bands and correlated insulators, with Bistritzer, MacDonald and Jarillo-Herrero. That is a clean theory-then-experiment story, and I agree with your widening to three names, because the flat-band prediction is a joint paper. But the discoveries that follow, such as fractional Chern insulators in moire systems, will be better judged in a few years, and I would not move B017 into my top choices now.

responses.point: Stefan prefers B041 and says that the support from members with different specialities makes him trust it more, while his own alternative list is B034 and B028, and he calls the attribution of B034 contested (Chu absent, Mlynek, Keith and Borde overlaps).
responses.response: I agree with your reading of the cross-field support, and I would add that the reproducibility test you apply as an experimentalist is the same one I apply as a theorist: the clock has been rebuilt and compared in laboratories that compete with one another. On B034 I share your doubt, even though I ranked it fifth and listed it among my alternatives. Atom interferometry is a beautiful and well-reproduced technique, but the credit is exactly as messy as you say. Chu is absent from the trio, and Mlynek, Keith and the early Bordé work overlap, so we would be making a priority judgement that the record does not make for us. I also agree with you that B034 does not work as a second part, because it would push the union above three names. I keep it as a fallback alternative because of its scientific merit, not because I think the credit is ready. I would ask you whether you accept the citation I proposed, since it follows your own wording on the magic-wavelength lattice.

responses.point: Eva O. wants the prize to rest on the historical record of who did the original experiment, notes that Katori made the first strontium demonstration, and says that other groups' accuracy work cannot be reflected in a two-person prize.
responses.response: Your emphasis on the historical record is the right standard, and it supports a two-name credit. Katori proposed the magic-wavelength idea and demonstrated it in strontium, and Ye took it to the 10^-18 regime, so the pair covers the invention and the state-of-the-art realisation. I would keep the citation from claiming that these two alone made the clock accurate. That is why my wording says the invention of the lattice clock and its realisation at the 10^-18 level, and does not say that they developed all of precision lattice metrology. On the other groups, I would not rule out a sentence in the committee's popular and scientific background that credits SYRTE, PTB and NIST for the accuracy evaluations and the clock comparisons. That is the usual way for the committee to acknowledge work beyond the three-person limit. I do not see a need for a second part to do this, and I agree with Johansson's point from the chair's summary that a second part would push the union beyond three people.

uncertainties: Whether Danielsson and Eriksson regard a precision-measurement prize as acceptable this year, given the 2005 and 2012 AMO prizes.

Whether the wording on the magic-wavelength lattice and the light-shift cancellation is enough to separate this prize from the 2005 and 2012 citations, or whether the committee will want it more narrowly drawn.
Priority details for Lemonde, Takamoto and Derevianko, and the latest accuracy records and the state of the redefinition of the second, which I give from memory and have not checked.
Whether a B004 trio can be made fair given Bernevig, Hughes, Zhang and Hasan, and whether the 2016 prize overlaps it.
statement.conflict_note: I am a long-time close collaborator of Anne L'Huillier (2023 laureate) and have worked with the Lund and ETH attosecond groups, but neither Katori nor Ye is a collaborator, so I see no conflict for B041. I also work in precision atomic physics and have disclosed that this may bias me towards the clock. Nothing in the round 1 exchange changes my disclosure. As I said earlier, I would ask the committee secretary to confirm that no recusal is needed for B002, B034 and B042, which I rank or list as alternatives and which do not form part of my final configuration.
